Controleren en veilig gebruiken Hoe de s:
Verifying and using safely

How the seed is calculated
  1. All rolls as digits in a row (spaces removed), e.g. 3615243362....
  2. SHA-256 over that text (ASCII). Every roll counts, however many there are.
  3. The first 128 bits (12 words) or all 256 bits (24 words) are the entropy.
  4. Standard BIP39: checksum = first ENT/32 bits of SHA-256(entropy), then groups of 11 bits map to the English wordlist.
  5. Master fingerprint: BIP39 seed via PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 (2048 rounds, salt "mnemonic" + passphrase), BIP32 master key via HMAC-SHA512("Bitcoin seed"), public key on secp256k1, first 4 bytes of RIPEMD-160(SHA-256(pubkey)). The PBKDF2 result is checked against WebCrypto. The fingerprint is not a secret and stays visible when hidden.
  6. Compact SeedQR: the same entropy (16 or 32 bytes) as a QR code in byte mode, error correction L, version 1 (21 x 21) or version 2 (25 x 25). The QR is read back and checked after it is made.

This is the same method as Ian Coleman BIP39 with Entropy Type = Base 10 and as the Bitcoin Seed Tool with Dice. With Ian in base 10, ignore the entropy counter: it counts 3 bits per roll and therefore overestimates.

With playing cards only step 1 differs: the input is the card sequence in the notation below (see "Playing cards"). Steps 2 to 6 are the same.

Playing cards: procedure, calculation and checks

Notation and calculation

  1. Each card becomes two characters: rank A 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 T J Q K (T = 10) and suit S spades ♠, H hearts ♥, C clubs ♣, D diamonds ♦.
  2. All cards of all rounds in a row, in the order entered, separated by exactly one space, with no space at the start or end. For example AS TH 9D QC .... Line breaks in the input field do not count; the exact text is under "Technical details".
  3. SHA-256 over that text (ASCII). After that exactly as with dice: the first 128 or 256 bits are the entropy.

How many cards and why a full deck

  • A perfectly shuffled deck has 52! possible orders: log2(52!) = 225.6 bits. For 12 words (128 bits) one round is needed, for 24 words (256 bits) two rounds of 52 (451 bits). The margin is a factor of 1.76 in both cases. Extra full rounds are allowed; they count.
  • The 52nd card of a round adds no entropy, because it is fixed. It does serve as a check: each card must appear exactly once per round. A duplicate or forgotten card is therefore always noticed.
  • This tool deliberately does not calculate with "draw and replace". Then you must reshuffle thoroughly after every card, 23 to 45 times or more. In practice that becomes a cut or a brief mix, which yields far less than the 5.7 bits per card the calculation assumes. A card entered twice also goes unnoticed with that method.

The shuffle is the weak point

  • With dice every roll is a new, independent event. With cards everything depends on how thoroughly you shuffle, and you cannot see that from the result.
  • Riffling (letting two halves of the deck zip together): according to the research of Bayer and Diaconis (1992) a deck is well mixed after about 7 riffles; after 3 or 4 there is still clear structure. Overhand shuffling alone (packets from one hand to the other) is much less effective: it takes thousands of shuffles. A common alternative is to slide the cards face down across the table for a minute.
  • Preferably do not start from a new, sorted deck without extra mixing first: a half-shuffled sorted deck does show up in the check below, a half-shuffled random deck does not.
  • The margin of 1.76 absorbs a somewhat sloppy shuffle, not a deck that was hardly shuffled.

Automatic checks

  • Each card exactly once per round; only full rounds of 52.
  • Consecutive cards of the same suit and adjacent rank (e.g. 7♥ 8♥ or 8♥ 7♥), the remnant of a sorted deck: with a good shuffle on average 1.8 per round. Warning from 6 (chance with a good shuffle about 1%), strong warning from 8 (about 0.05%).
  • From round 2: cards that are next to each other again as in the previous round (in the same or reverse order), a sign of too little reshuffling. With a good shuffle on average 2. Warning from 7 (about 0.3%), strong warning from 8 (about 0.07%).
  • These checks only catch gross errors. No warning does not mean the shuffle was good.

Recomputing in a second tool

Ian Coleman's card mode uses a different notation (with the symbols ♠ ♥ ♦ ♣) and calculates the entropy as if cards are replaced. It therefore gives different words. Recompute like this:

  1. Take the input under "Technical details" and calculate the SHA-256, for example in the Terminal: printf '%s' 'AS TH 9D ...' | shasum -a 256 (Linux: sha256sum). It must equal "SHA-256(input)" in this tool.
  2. Take the first 32 hex characters (12 words) or all 64 (24 words) and enter them in Ian Coleman: Entropy, type Hex, Mnemonic Length Use Raw Entropy. Same words = neither tool has manipulated your input.

"Test cards (random)" button

Only for trying out the tool. Shuffles virtually with Fisher-Yates on crypto.getRandomValues, rejecting values above the largest multiple so that every order is exactly equally likely, with no fallback to Math.random. Fills in exactly the required number of rounds. The result is marked red as TESTSEED, just like test rolls.

How the randomizer works ("Test rolls (random)" button)

The button only exists to try the tool quickly without rolling. A seed from test rolls is never meant for real value.

  1. Source. crypto.getRandomValues: the browser's cryptographic random generator, which takes its randomness from the operating system (see below). If it is not available, the button refuses. There is no fallback to Math.random.
  2. From byte to roll. The browser supplies bytes from 0 to 255. Bytes of 252 and above are discarded, the rest become 1 + (byte mod 6). Because 252 = 42 x 6, each face occurs exactly 42 out of 252 times: exactly 1/6, without the slight preference a plain remainder would give. On average 1.6% of the bytes are dropped; more are drawn until the count is right.
  3. Count. Exactly the recommended number for the chosen length: 100 rolls for 12 words, 199 for 24 words. They are placed in the input field in groups of 5, as if you had typed them yourself.
  4. After that, nothing special. From the input field, test rolls follow exactly the same path as real rolls: quality analysis, SHA-256, BIP39. So the randomizer does not make a seed, it only fills in rolls. That also lets you practise the check in a second tool: the test rolls in Ian Coleman (Base 10) give the same words.
  5. Marking. The input, the result, the fingerprint, the enlarged SeedQR, the address QR and the xpub QR get the label TESTSEED. The checkbox for confirming a weak input is cleared. The marking stays if you change or add rolls afterwards, because the input then remains largely machine-made. It only disappears with an empty input field, "Wipe everything", an entered existing seed or leaving the page.

Where the randomness comes from

crypto.getRandomValues invents nothing itself. Chrome, Firefox and Safari take the bytes from the operating system's generator: on macOS via CommonCrypto (CCRandomGenerateBytes), on Linux via getrandom or /dev/urandom, on Windows via the system RNG. That generator is fed with noise from the hardware (interrupts, timing and, on modern processors, a hardware RNG) and then passed through a cryptographic algorithm. It is the same source that also makes SSH keys, TLS connections and disk encryption. The exact function differs per browser and OS version.

The opposite is Math.random: fast, but not cryptographic. From a handful of outputs the rest can be predicted. This page does not use that function anywhere.

How reliable: what is

  • As a source of randomness it is excellent, better than dice: no biased faces, no rounded corners, no counting or typing errors.
  • As far as known, there has been no practical attack in recent years on getRandomValues itself in a major browser.
  • This page fails closed: without getRandomValues the button refuses, there is no fallback.

How reliable: what is not

  • Cannot be tested. A generator seeded with only 40 bits passes every statistical test; the output looks just as random. You cannot tell from a seed whether the generator was good. You can only rely on three things: that this file is genuine (SHA-256), that browser and operating system have not been tampered with, and that there is no silent fallback anywhere in the code.
  • It went wrong in the layer above. The known disasters were not in the browser generator, but in code around it:
    • Randstorm (public 2023): old JavaScript wallet code (jsbn) fell back to Math.random in browsers of that time. Wallets from roughly 2011 to 2015 are weak as a result.
    • CryptoJS (CVE-2026-71851, exploitation discovered May 2026): versions before 4.0.0 used their own generator, seeded with Math.random. A 128-bit key had only about 239 possibilities; wallets and browser extensions were drained.
    • Coldcard (2026): silent fallback to a weak internal generator in a hardware wallet.
    Always the same pattern: a fallback to a weak source that nobody notices.
  • The bottom layer is not sacred. Rare, but it has happened: with Debian/OpenSSL (2008) a change in the operating system made all keys predictable for two years. A virtual machine restored from a snapshot can also repeat its generator state. On a normal computer or a freshly booted live USB this does not apply.
  • A modified copy of this page can take "random" rolls from a sequence known to the attacker. That cannot be seen from the result.
  • The rolls are on the screen and in the memory of a computer that may be or may have been online.

Compared with dice

Browser RNGDice
Quality of the randomnessBetterGood enough with 100/199 rolls
VerifiableNoYes, recompute in a second tool
Can fail unnoticedYesNo: what you roll and type, you see yourself

Conclusion. As a source of randomness the browser RNG is better than your dice, but still the worse choice for a seed with real value, because you cannot demonstrate that it worked correctly. For this test button it is more than sufficient. If you do not want to use dice, a hardware wallet's generator is a better choice than this button; it is just as unverifiable, which is the lesson of Coldcard.

Why these minimums
  • A perfect die yields log2(6) = 2.585 bits per roll. Cheap dice are never perfect.
  • The hard lower limit therefore calculates conservatively with 2.32 bits per roll (log2 5). That is what remains if one face even has a 20% chance instead of 16.7%. Even with such a skewed die you reach the full 128 or 256 bits.
  • Minimum: 56 rolls for 12 words, 111 rolls for 24 words. Below that the tool refuses.
  • Recommended: 2x the required entropy with a fair die (100 and 199 rolls respectively). More rolls never hurt: SHA-256 compresses everything into the required bits, extra rolls only increase the margin.
Procedure for real money
  1. Check the SHA-256 of this HTML file against SHA256SUMS in the release at github.com/jurgen2005/dice-seed-bip39/releases, or rebuild the file yourself from the source there (python3 build.py) and compare.
  2. Use an offline computer, preferably booted from a live USB (e.g. Tails), without network.
  3. Roll a good die (a casino die is ideal). Really roll it: shake it in your hand or a cup and let it roll, do not place it or redo a roll. Write the rolls down on paper first.
  4. Or use playing cards: a complete deck, at least 7 riffles, and for 24 words a second round after reshuffling thoroughly. See "Playing cards" above.
  5. Check the result in a second, independent tool (Ian Coleman, Entropy, Base 10, same length). Same words = neither tool has manipulated your input. With playing cards via the SHA-256 and Hex, as described under "Playing cards".
  6. Write the words on paper or metal. No photo, no screenshot, no copy/paste. If you want to keep the Compact SeedQR: copy it by hand onto a SeedQR template (turn on the grid), do not print it on a network printer.
  7. Click "Wipe everything", close the browser and shut down the computer.
  8. Consider a strong BIP39 passphrase as an extra layer.
  9. The "Test rolls (random)" button is only for trying out the tool. Those rolls come from the browser RNG, exactly the kind of source you want to avoid with dice. A test seed is marked red.
